items.title: [space.com] ISS astronauts install seventh upgraded solar array during 100th US spacewalk
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed and unfurled the International Space Station’s seventh upgraded roll-out solar array on Oct. 29, completing a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk that marked the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station. The new panel adds about 8 kilowatts of power to support station operations as the original arrays lose output after exceeding their 15-year design life. The crew used the Canadarm2 robotic arm to move the array to its mounting point and connected it to power channel 2A. The new arrays supplement, rather than replace, the station’s original solar wings; together, they are expected to raise available power to about 215 kilowatts. The extra capacity will support research, life-support systems and visiting spacecraft through the station’s planned 2030 retirement and controlled deorbit. The crew also completed preparatory work for the eighth and final array. Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to install it on Nov. 5, completing the five-year upgrade.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Climate tracker projects 857,000 heat deaths as Super El Niño intensifies
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A University of Chicago Climate Impact Lab tracker projects about 857,400 additional heat-related deaths worldwide from June 2026 through March 2027 as a Super El Niño develops. It estimates 484,500 excess deaths from June through September and forecasts another 372,900 over the next six months. The projected toll rose after August and September were warmer than the lab had forecast. The figures are model estimates, not confirmed death counts. The tracker projects the highest additional death tolls in India, Nigeria and China over the full period, with Nigeria forecast to have the most deaths in the next six months. Sea temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific’s Niño 3.4 region were 3.4°C above usual levels during Oct. 18-24, and the World Meteorological Organization expects the event to become much stronger than a typical El Niño between November and January. Health experts warn that women and girls may spend more time collecting water and providing care during extreme heat, while unreliable electricity and unsafe housing can make heat advice difficult to follow.

Scotland’s summer of 2026 brought earlier harvests, heat stress in spring-sown crops and rapidly falling water levels, while research indicates extreme day-to-night temperature swings have become more frequent since the 1980s. Those swings can disrupt crop growth. The Scotsman reported Scottish cereal yields below historic averages, with results varying by crop, soil and location. A Swedish research project is testing a retention-irrigation system that stores water during dry periods and releases it during floods to develop recommendations for its use. In Spain, agricultural cooperatives say farmers are working to adapt and cut emissions but warn that putting innovations into practice depends on farm profitability and adequate funding under the next EU farm-policy reform.

items.title: [theguardian.com] California high tides flood coastal roads as El Niño risks grow
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Record October tides flooded roads, homes and businesses along California’s coast this week, prompting warnings that storms during El Niño could worsen flooding. In Marin County, drivers were rescued from flooded cars and kayakers crossed streets; in Newport Beach, flooding blocked access to a local boat company’s dock. Researchers attribute the high water to rising seas, unusually warm ocean water, El Niño-linked Kelvin waves and the lunar tide cycle. Higher tides are predicted for December, when king tides and winter storms could bring further coastal flooding, though the effects will depend on their timing. The San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission is using risk maps to help local officials plan, while Newport Beach is distributing sandbags.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [esa.int] Hubble and Webb expose hidden structures in Carina star-forming cloud
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes have captured complementary views of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a star-forming pillar in the Carina Nebula about 7,500 light-years from Earth. Hubble’s visible-light image shows a dark dust column edged by glowing gas, while Webb’s infrared observations reveal details within the dust, including stars and fine strands. The images, released Oct. 29, help astronomers examine how young stars form in gas and dust exposed to radiation from massive nearby stars. Ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds likely shaped the pillar’s outline by eroding its surroundings, while denser material resisted erosion. Webb also imaged the lower-metallicity N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, while Chandra and Webb observations show young stars forming in a separate Carina cloud.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.

Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government released “The Plan for a Stronger Canada,” the country’s first national security strategy in more than two decades, placing economic security alongside foreign policy, defence, public safety and intelligence. It identifies eight sectors in which to build Canadian capacity, including emerging technologies, critical minerals, energy, defence, pharmaceuticals and food security, and says the country must prepare for all contingencies, including war. The 13-page framework argues that reliance on global trade and foreign systems can leave Canada vulnerable to economic shocks and coercion. It calls for stronger domestic capabilities and partnerships with allies. The strategy does not identify any country as a threat; the United States is the only country it names. Ottawa plans five more detailed policies, starting with a foreign policy expected in about a month, and says it will propose changes to national security laws within a year. The government also plans a first ministers’ meeting on security, likely next year, and a review of the national security enterprise within four years.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Astronomers say ED138's dwarf-planet status awaits size measurements
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Astronomers say 2026 ED138, an icy object beyond Pluto and a potential dwarf planet, cannot be classified until researchers measure its size more accurately. Its estimated diameter ranges from 600 to 1,500 kilometers, and Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, said the measurements may take months. The uncertainty arises because astronomers infer size from reflected sunlight: a small, bright object can appear as luminous as a larger, darker one. Infrared observations and longer-wavelength measurements with facilities such as Chile’s Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) could help narrow the size estimate; ALMA can detect light emitted by the object itself. If the body is large enough for its gravity to make it nearly round, it could qualify as the sixth dwarf planet recognized by the International Astronomical Union; the current size estimate alone does not establish its shape or status. Further observations will refine its size estimate, leaving astronomers and the Union to determine its classification.

Data-center construction is creating union jobs in Nevada, while automation cuts or threatens positions in hospitality and customer service and employers in other sectors increase output without expanding headcount. A report by the Maine Center for Economic Policy found little evidence of widespread AI-related job losses in the state so far, while a survey of Swiss finance chiefs found 64% expect fewer entry-level finance jobs over the next three years. In Nevada, self-driving vehicles, casino robots and digital guest services are changing work on the Las Vegas Strip as thousands of tradespeople build data centers near Reno. Analysts and researchers warn that companies may reduce junior hiring because AI handles basic tasks that traditionally helped new workers gain experience. A survey cited by MIT Technology Review Insights found 16% of respondents saw transformative value from AI, while 12% had agents in production. U.S. federal AI regulation remains stalled in Congress, but a local report said the next Congress could take it up in January. China’s State Council issued guidance on Oct. 23 to limit employment displacement and support worker transitions.
